building_blocks.desc: Overhead lines double circuit single tower, twin conductor per phase. Rating calculated for summer day, 1m/s wind speed, and air temperature of 35oC.
building_blocks.nt:
1. Plant amount includes: Strain + Structural tower associated costs (steel tower with single earth peak, structural foundation steel, foundation leg steel, climbing barrier, fittings, insulators) and insulator and conductor. 85% suspension, 15% strain and 400m span. Sag and OPGW has been appropriately assigned
2. Civil and structural works includes: Tower concrete footing, soil tests, installation of tower and foundations
3. Electrical works includes: installation of conductor (setup, draw wires,stringing, clamping off), installation of OHEW/OPGW (draw wire, stringing, clamping off)
4. Secondary system and testing and commissioning is accounted in the terminating end in the substation switchbay cost

building_blocks.desc: Transformers and associated civil, structural, electrical and secondary system
building_blocks.nt:
1. Plant amount includes: transformer and surge arrester 
2. Civil and structural works includes: foundation, drainage building, firewall, all civil work for control cabling, gantry and busbar
3. Electrical works includes: cabling, termination, control panel, bus connection, installation of surge arrestor and earth switch, and marshalling kiosk
4. Secondary systems includes: control panel equipments
5. Design and survey includes: civil design, primary design, secondary design, protection setting etc 
6. Contractor project management and overheads is allocated $0 at individual major plant level because it will be accounted for overall in the substation level building block

1. Plant amount includes: Reactor unit
2. Civil and structural works includes: AIS/outdoor, fencing, drainage, all civil work for control cabling, footing.  [Busbar is accounted for in the corresponding switchbay protecting this plant]
3. Electrical works includes: Cabling, termination, control panel, bus connection, surge arrestor install, earth switch install, marshalling kiosk
4. Secondary systems includes: control panel equipments
5. Design and survey includes: Civil design, primary design, secondary design, power quality/stability parameter setting
6. Contractor project management and overheads is allocated $0 at individual major plant level because it will be accounted for overall in the substation level building block

building_blocks.desc: Lump sum allowance for the entire project. This building block estimate is a network element by itself and accounts for all other constituiting network elements. SPS estimate excludes non-network or BESS solutions
building_blocks.nt: SPS are a subset of SIPS and are network solutions and will also be needed to the extent required to control non-network solutions. This building block cost estimate is applicable for the entire project (consisting of multiple network elements) and should be included by itself if it is required. SPS is over and above the traditional control, protection and comms system installed and embedded as part of standard building blocks. SPS may leverage existing/estimated assets such as OPGW, CT and other secondary system items which have already been accounted for in other network element building blocks. The objective of the SPS is to keep various parts of NEM operating securely following the non-credible loss of interconnectors and large generators and preventing cascading power outages. Use the 'station' category project attributes, known and unknown risk factors to adjust this estimated cost to suit your specific project

The objective of the SPS is to keep various parts of NEM operating securely following the non-credible loss of interconnectors and large generators and preventing cascading power outages. Use the 'substation' category project attributes, known and unknown risk factors to adjust this estimated cost to suit your specific project

adjustments.desc: This project attribute choice accounts for work productivity while delivering the project. Challenging terrain slows down project work

The terrain topography should be considered on a larger/wider area rather than small and immediate changes to the contour lines

adjustments.desc: This project attribute choice accounts for work productivity while delivering the project. Challenging terrain slows down project work

The terrain topography should be considered on a larger/wider area rather than small and immediate changes to the contour lines

adjustments.desc: This project attribute choice assigns appropriate cost depending on risk and benefit profile of the chosen model

In D&C contracts direct procurement can be less, but indirect overheads increase. TNSP's are required to select the most efficient delivery model.

risks.desc: This known risk factor choice accounts for general social and economic condition. It costs more to deliver projects in restricted or uncertain economic and social environments.
risks.nt: A stable political, economical and social situation across the supply chain of resoucres exist. Australia is a stable country and BAU is default in most cases.

risks.desc: This known risk factor choice accounts for general social and economic condition. It costs more to deliver projects in restricted or uncertain economic and social environments.

risks.desc: This known risk factor choice accounts for general social and economic condition. It costs more to deliver projects in restricted or uncertain economic and social environments.

risks.desc: This known risk factor choice accounts for general market condition. It costs more to deliver project with restricted supply and unavailability of resources

risks.desc: This unknown risk factor should be chosen if compiling early stage (Class 5b) cost estimate for project network elements using concept level scoping with no site-specific review or TNSP input. We expect this to be the most common usage of the TCD. This factor attempts to compensate the accuracy offset (underestimation) observed in the early stage cost estimate of recent NEM projects due to scope creep in the project definition as it matures to advance stage.
risks.nt:
Examples of scope creep in a station project as it matures are as follow. These factors are unknown at early stage but experience suggest they often do occur in major/complex projects.
•	Road improvements / access tracks not considered in early stages
•	Delivery scope and conditions not fully understood at early definition stage
•	Changes in legislation and standards

risks.desc: This unknown risk factor should be chosen if compiling early stage (Class 5a) cost estimate for project network elements using screening level scoping including high level site-specific review and TNSP input. This factor attempts to compensate the accuracy offset (underestimation) observed in the early stage cost estimate of recent NEM projects due to scope creep in the project definition as it matures to advance stage.
risks.nt:
Examples of scope creep in a station project as it matures are as follow. These factors are unknown at early stage but experience suggest they often do occur in major/complex projects.
•	Road improvements / access tracks not considered in early stages
•	Delivery scope and conditions not fully understood at early definition stage
•	Changes in legislation and standards

risks.desc: Do not choose this unknown risk factor if only compiling early stage (Class 5) cost estimate for network elements using the provided building block estimates in this TCD and with limited attribute and risk information. This unknown risk factor is to be used only when the user has an improved knowledge of scope of work and site specific attribute and risk profile resulting in bespoke and confident scope of work. It is expected that such knowledge will result in more varieties and quantities of assets than estimating with Class 5 knowledge (i.e. the magnitude of known cost is more at this stage). For e.g. the station now includes bespoke configuration of switchbay with additional/more surge arrestors than allowed for in the standard building block in the TCD. This factor attempts to compensate the accuracy offset (underestimation) observed in the Class 4 cost estimate of recent NEM projects due to scope creep in the project definition as it matures to advance stage.
risks.nt:
Examples of scope creep in a station project as it matures are as follow. These factors are unknown at early stage but experience suggest they often do occur in major/complex projects.
•	Road improvements / access tracks not considered in early stages
•	Delivery scope and conditions not fully understood at early definition stage
•	Changes in legislation and standards

risks.desc: Do not choose this unknown risk factor if only compiling early stage (Class 5) cost estimate for network elements using the provided building block estimates in this TCD and with limited attribute and risk information. This unknown risk factor is to be used only when the user has an advance knowledge of scope of work and site specific attribute and risk profile resulting in bespoke and definitive scope of work. It is expected that such knowledge will result in even more varieties and quantities of assets than estimating with Class 4 knowledge (i.e. the magnitude of known cost is even more at this stage). For e.g. the station now includes bigger car park area than allowed for in the standard building block in the TCD. At Class 3, this factor is negligible and it is expected that such scope creep does not remain unknown. A very small correction factor is applied as the project has now matured and the scope is now deemed advance.
risks.nt:
Examples of scope creep in a station project as it matures are as follow. These factors are unknown at early stage but experience suggest they often do occur in major/complex projects.
•	Road improvements / access tracks not considered in early stages
•	Delivery scope and conditions not fully understood at early definition stage
•	Changes in legislation and standards

risks.desc: Class 1/2 estimate represents 'contractual' cost and is beyond the scope of the TCD. At this stage, it is expected that all the unknown risk factors have materialised, mitigated or avoided and that there are no surprises left in the project. No factor is applied to the compiled cost estimate.
risks.nt:
Examples of scope creep in a station project as it matures are as follow. These factors are unknown at early stage but experience suggest they often do occur in major/complex projects.
•	Road improvements / access tracks not considered in early stages
•	Delivery scope and conditions not fully understood at early definition stage
•	Changes in legislation and standards

risks.desc: This known risk factor choice accounts for general social and economic condition. It costs more to deliver projects in restricted or uncertain economic and social environments.
risks.nt: Some/minor degree of political, economical and social restriction or uncertainty across the supply chain of resources exist. For e.g. commodity price and wage indices growth rate and forex expected to be above historical trend.

risks.desc: This known risk factor choice accounts for general social and economic condition. It costs more to deliver projects in restricted or uncertain economic and social environments.
risks.nt: Heightened degree of political, economical and social restriction or uncertainty across the supply chain of resoucres exist. For e.g. commodity price and wage indices growth rate and forex expected to be much higher than historical trend.

risks.desc: This known risk factor choice accounts for general market condition. It costs more to deliver project with restricted supply and unavailability of resources
risks.nt: In this choice the supply of the resources exceed the demand in the market and hence the competition lowers the cost estimate

risks.desc: This known risk factor choice accounts for general market condition. It costs more to deliver project with restricted supply and unavailability of resources
risks.nt: In this choice the supply matches the demand for the resources and the building block cost estimate already incorporates this BAU scenario. No adjustment is made

risks.desc: This known risk factor choice accounts for general market condition. It costs more to deliver project with restricted supply and unavailability of resources
risks.nt: In this choice the demand for the resources exceed the supply in the market and hence the need pushes up the cost estimate

risks.desc: This known risk factor choice assigns appropriate cost depending on available knowledge for the given nature of the project
risks.nt: This choice represents the existence of the organisational knowledge and confidence level to deliver the given project

risks.desc: This known risk factor choice assigns appropriate cost depending on available knowledge for the given nature of the project
risks.nt: This choice represents limited existence of the organisational knowledge and the some additional need and time to develop, study and design the project delivery. Industry wide such knowledge and experience is available. Very few Australian project precedent in recent history

risks.desc: This known risk factor choice assigns appropriate cost depending on available knowledge for the given nature of the project
risks.nt: This choice represents non-existence of the organisational knowledge and the additional need and time to develop, study and design the project delivery. Industry wide such knowledge and experience is also very rare. No Australian project precedent in recent history

risks.desc: This known risk factor assigns appropriate cost depending on the type of easement acquisition needed. The cost of acquiring easement is influenced by how early the easement could be acquired before the in-service date. This is best categorised as Low, Expected Historically or High. For greenfield work it is expected that the project proponent will avoid this risk factor by considering prudent/alternate routes
risks.nt: This choice lowers the expected easement/property cost estimate

risks.desc: This known risk factor assigns appropriate cost depending on the type of easement acquisition needed. The cost of acquiring easement is influenced by how early the easement could be acquired before the in-service date. This is best categorised as Low, Expected Historically or High. For greenfield work it is expected that the project proponent will avoid this risk factor by considering prudent/alternate routes
risks.nt: The building block estimate incorporates historical project experiences (i.e. BAU) and as such this choice does not adjust the already made easement/property cost estimate

risks.desc: This known risk factor assigns appropriate cost depending on the type of easement acquisition needed. The cost of acquiring easement is influenced by how early the easement could be acquired before the in-service date. This is best categorised as Low, Expected Historically or High. For greenfield work it is expected that the project proponent will avoid this risk factor by considering prudent/alternate routes
risks.nt: This choice increase the expected easement/property cost estimate. A strong justification is needed if a greenfield site has 'high' compulsory acquisition risk

risks.desc: This known risk factor choice assigns appropriate cost depending on the nature of property/easement requirement. For greenfield work it is expected that the project proponent will not choose route with high environmental offset risks. Such factors should be mitigated by considering prudent/alternate route options
risks.nt: This choice adjust the already made environmental offset cost estimate in the building blocks by some degree commensurating with the site. This is to compensate for unavoidable impacts on significant environmental matters (e.g. valuable species and ecosystems) on one site, by securing or paying for land at another site, and for managing that land over a period of time, to replace those significant environmental matters which were lost.

risks.desc: This known risk factor choice assigns appropriate cost depending on the nature of property/easement requirement. For greenfield work it is expected that the project proponent will not choose route with high environmental offset risks. Such factors should be mitigated by considering prudent/alternate route options
risks.nt: This choice adjust the already made environmental offset cost estimate in the building blocks. This is to compensate for unavoidable impacts on significant environmental matters (e.g. valuable species and ecosystems) on one site, by securing or paying for land at another site, and for managing that land over a period of time, to replace those significant environmental matters which were lost.

risks.desc: This known risk factor choice assigns appropriate cost depending on the nature of property/easement requirement. For greenfield work it is expected that the project proponent will not choose route with high environmental offset risks. Such factors should be mitigated by considering prudent/alternate route options
risks.nt: This choice adjust the already made environmental offset cost estimate in the building blocks commensurating with a high risk. This is to compensate for unavoidable impacts on significant environmental matters (e.g. valuable species and ecosystems) on one site, by securing or paying for land at another site, and for managing that land over a period of time, to replace those significant environmental matters which were lost. However, if this is a greenfield site and this factor is deemed 'high', this choice needs to be supported by a strong justification

risks.desc: This known risk factor choice impacts civil works and associated estimates due to favourable/unfavourable geotechnical condition on work site such as ground water level, asbestos contamination, soil/rock type for excavation etc.
risks.nt: This choice lowers the expected civil works and associated cost estimates. For e.g. excavation productivity is much greater in clay soil than in granite ground. Choose this option if the soil/ground condition is favouable for earthwork activity (dry load bearing soil, no asbestos, no movement etc.)

risks.desc: This known risk factor choice impacts civil works and associated estimates due to favourable/unfavourable geotechnical condition on work site such as ground water level, asbestos contamination, soil/rock type for excavation etc.
risks.nt: The building block estimate incorporates historical project experiences corresponding with BAU risk level and as such this choice does not adjust the already made civil works and associated cost estimates

risks.desc: This known risk factor choice impacts civil works and associated estimates due to favourable/unfavourable geotechnical condition on work site such as ground water level, asbestos contamination, soil/rock type for excavation etc.
risks.nt: This choice increases the expected civil works and associated cost estimates. For e.g. excavation productivity is much lower in granite ground. Choose this option if the soil/ground condition is unfavouable for earthwork activity (high water level, asbestos presence, ground movement etc.)

risks.desc: This known risk factor choice accounts for availability to work on deenergised asset and connection activities. HV connection work to live system/grid usually needs planned outage
risks.nt: Planned outage is easily available and operationally it cost less that the allowance made for in the building block estimates

risks.desc: This known risk factor choice accounts for availability to work on deenergised asset and connection activities. HV connection work to live system/grid usually needs planned outage
risks.nt: Planned outage needs advance work and operational coordination. The already estimated building block cost incorporate this BAU scenario

risks.desc: This known risk factor choice accounts for availability to work on deenergised asset and connection activities. HV connection work to live system/grid usually needs planned outage
risks.nt: Planned outage is not available or difficult/long to coordinate. Operationally it cost more that the allowance made for in the building block estimates

risks.desc: This known risk factor continues to exist during delivery stage and the choice impacts the productivity/schedule. Outdoor work activities are exposed to elements and are restricted by safety compliances
risks.nt: In this choice the weather condition is expected to be favourable allowing quicker/productive work. However, underground cabling work due to its nature is not impacted much by such scenario

risks.desc: This known risk factor continues to exist during delivery stage and the choice impacts the productivity/schedule. Outdoor work activities are exposed to elements and are restricted by safety compliances
risks.nt: In this choice the usual weather conditions is expected and the building block cost estimate already incorporates this BAU scenario. No adjustment is made. For e.g. multi-year scope of work is exposed to seasonal variance and therefore will experience the usual condition and delays in a given year

risks.desc: This known risk factor continues to exist during delivery stage and the choice impacts the productivity/schedule. Outdoor work activities are exposed to elements and are restricted by safety compliances
risks.nt: In this choice the weather condition is expected to be unfavourable resulting in slower/unproductive work and hence the higher cost estimate for outdoor works. For e.g. work activity are mostly outdoor and performed in unfavourable season of the year or located in extreme climatic regions (wet weather, flooding)

risks.desc: This known risk factor choice assigns appropriate cost depending on the nature of easement requirement
risks.nt: This choice does not adjust the already made building block cost estimates to mitigate cultural heritage issues

risks.desc: This known risk factor choice assigns appropriate cost depending on the nature of easement requirement
risks.nt: This choice slightly impacts the already made building block cost estimates to mitigate cultural heritage issues which is BAU project experience

risks.desc: This known risk factor choice assigns appropriate cost depending on the nature of easement requirement
risks.nt: This choice impacts the already made building block cost estimates to mitigate cultural heritage issues

risks.desc: This unknown risk factor should be chosen if compiling early stage (Class 5b) cost estimate for project network elements using concept level scoping with no site-specific review or TNSP input. We expect this to be the most common usage of the TCD. This factor attempts to compensate the accuracy offset (underestimation) observed in the early stage cost estimate of recent NEM projects due to scope creep in the project definition as it matures to advance stage.
risks.nt:
Examples of scope creep in an underground cable project as it matures are as follow. These factors are unknown at early stage but experience suggest they often do occur in major/complex projects.
•	City council reinstatement and road improvement requirement not considered in early stages
•	Route deviations not understood at early stage
•	Degree of risk with road, rail, utility interfaces not understood at early stage
•	Delivery scope and conditions not fully understood at early definition stage
•	Changes in legislation and standards

risks.desc: This unknown risk factor should be chosen if compiling early stage (Class 5a) cost estimate for project network elements using screening level scoping including high level site-specific review and TNSP input. This factor attempts to compensate the accuracy offset (underestimation) observed in the early stage cost estimate of recent NEM projects due to scope creep in the project definition as it matures to advance stage.
risks.nt:
Examples of scope creep in an underground cable project as it matures are as follow. These factors are unknown at early stage but experience suggest they often do occur in major/complex projects.
•	City council reinstatement and road improvement requirement not considered in early stages
•	Route deviations not understood at early stage
•	Degree of risk with road, rail, utility interfaces not understood at early stage
•	Delivery scope and conditions not fully understood at early definition stage
•	Changes in legislation and standards

risks.desc: Do not choose this unknown risk factor if only compiling early stage (Class 5) cost estimate for network elements using the provided building block estimates in this TCD and with limited attribute and risk information. This unknown risk factor is to be used only when the user has an improved knowledge of scope of work and site specific attribute and risk profile resulting in bespoke and confident scope of work. It is expected that such knowledge will result in more varieties and quantities of assets than estimating with Class 5 knowledge (i.e. the magnitude of known cost is more at this stage). For e.g. the underground cable now includes temperature monitoring system. This factor attempts to compensate the accuracy offset (underestimation) observed in the Class 4 cost estimate of recent NEM projects due to scope creep in the project definition as it matures to advance stage.
risks.nt:
Examples of scope creep in an underground cable project as it matures are as follow. These factors are unknown at early stage but experience suggest they often do occur in major/complex projects.
•	City council reinstatement and road improvement requirement not considered in early stages
•	Route deviations not understood at early stage
•	Degree of risk with road, rail, utility interfaces not understood at early stage
•	Delivery scope and conditions not fully understood at early definition stage
•	Changes in legislation and standards

risks.desc: Do not choose this unknown risk factor if only compiling early stage (Class 5) cost estimate for network elements using the provided building block estimates in this TCD and with limited attribute and risk information. This unknown risk factor is to be used only when the user has an advance knowledge of scope of work and site specific attribute and risk profile resulting in bespoke and definitive scope of work. It is expected that such knowledge will result in even more varieties and quantities of assets than estimating with Class 4 knowledge (i.e. the magnitude of known cost is even more at this stage). For e.g. the trenching for underground cable now needs to avoid/bypass certain geographical area to mitigate environmental risk thereby increasing the route distance. At Class 3, this factor is negligible and it is expected that such scope creep does not remain unknown. A very small correction factor is applied as the project has now matured and the scope is now deemed advance.
risks.nt:
Examples of scope creep in an underground cable project as it matures are as follow. These factors are unknown at early stage but experience suggest they often do occur in major/complex projects.
•	City council reinstatement and road improvement requirement not considered in early stages
•	Route deviations not understood at early stage
•	Degree of risk with road, rail, utility interfaces not understood at early stage
•	Delivery scope and conditions not fully understood at early definition stage
•	Changes in legislation and standards

risks.desc: Class 1/2 estimate represents 'contractual' cost and is beyond the scope of the TCD. At this stage, it is expected that all the unknown risk factors have materialised, mitigated or avoided and that there are no surprises left in the project. No factor is applied to the compiled cost estimate.
risks.nt:
Examples of scope creep in an underground cable project as it matures are as follow. These factors are unknown at early stage but experience suggest they often do occur in major/complex projects.
•	City council reinstatement and road improvement requirement not considered in early stages
•	Route deviations not understood at early stage
•	Degree of risk with road, rail, utility interfaces not understood at early stage
•	Delivery scope and conditions not fully understood at early definition stage
•	Changes in legislation and standards

risks.desc: The building block cost data is revised through benchmarking using past project estimates and completed project costs where available.  Building block costs are expected to be  more accurate where recent project data is more available/reliable.  This unknown risk factor should be chosen based on the uncertaintly of labour costs in building block costs being  5% to 10% too low.

• The building block costs were based on limited available data comparisons
• the forecast indexation is considered to be lower than expected

indirect_costs.cat: Indirect Cost (to be applied to overall total project network element capex estimate)
indirect_costs.desc: This indirect cost attribute choice reflects the overall/majority nature of the entire project. The user is required to input their choice/judgement considering the overall project and should generally align with their inputs for each individual network element attribute choice. This allow users to manually make this judgement at the project level and is useful where multiple network elements may have different attribute choices
indirect_costs.nt: The total indirect cost assigned to the overall project is the same irrespective of greenfield/brownfield status. However, the cost distribution within the constituting cost centres differs. This estimate of indirect costs is suitable for overall total project estimate of ≤$50m

The user is required to input their choice/judgement considering the overall project and should generally align with their inputs for each individual network element attribute choice. This allow users to manually make this judgement at the project level and is useful where multiple network elements may have different attribute choices
indirect_costs.nt: The total indirect cost assigned to the overall project is the same irrespective of greenfield/brownfield status. However, the cost distribution within the constituting cost centres differs. This estimate of indirect costs is suitable for overall total project estimate of >$500m to ≤$1000m
